body.p: This communication is responsive to the Office Action dated July 8, 2022. Applicant has not amended the claims. Claims 1-30 remain pending.

Applicant thanks the Examiner for the telephonic interview conducted on October 7, 2022. Participating in the interview were Examiners Michael J. Lau and Carl Layno, and Applicant's representative, Jason D. Kelly (Reg. No. 54,213). During the interview, the partiesdiscussed the rejection of claim 1 under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) and possible amendments. No exhibits were shown, and no agreements reached.

The Office Action stated that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) has been invoked when interpreting claims 1, 27, and 29. With respect to claims 1 and 27, the Office Action asserted that the phrase "processing circuitry configured to" invoked interpretation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) despite not including the word "means." Applicant respectfully disagrees. As noted in MPEP 2181, the term "circuitry" is a structural term that has been found by the Federal Circuit not to invoke interpretation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f).1
Claim Rejection Under 35 U.S.C. 4 112(b)

The Office Action rejected claims 1-30 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) as allegedly being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or joint inventor regards as the invention. Specifically, the Office Action stated "[r]egarding claim 1, 18, 27, and 29, it is unclear if the processing circuitry of the at least one of the insertable cardiac monitor or the remote computing device is located interior or exterior of the patient."2 Applicant respectfully disagrees that these claims are unclear.

Claim 1, for example, recites "processing circuitry of at least one of the insertable cardiac monitor or the remote computing device." Consequently, according to claim 1, the recited processing circuitry may be processing circuitry of the insertable cardiac monitor, processing
1 Citing, Mass.. Inst. Of Tech. v. Abacus Software, 462 F.3d 1344, 1354 (Fed. Cir. 2006).
2 Office Action dated July 8, 2022, page 5.

circuitry of the remote computing device, or processing circuitry of both the insertable cardiac monitor and the remote computing device. Consequently, when read in light of the specification as required, a person of ordinary skill in the art would readily understand that the processing circuity recited in claim 1 could include processing circuitry located interior to the patient, processing circuitry located exterior to the patient, or both processing circuitry located interior to the patient and processing circuitry located exterior to the patient.3

Applicant submits that claims 1-30 particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or joint inventor regards as the invention, in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration withdrawal of this rejection.
Claim Rejection Under 35 U.S.C. 4 102(a)(1)

The Office Action rejected claims 1-30 under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) as allegedly being anticipated by U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2005/0115561 by Stahmann et al. (hereinafter, "Stahmann"). Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection. In order to support an anticipation rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1), it is well established that a prior art reference must disclose each and every element of a claim. This well-known rule of law is commonly referred to as the "all-elements rule."4 If a prior art reference fails to disclose any element of a claim, then rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) is improper.5 Stahmann fails to disclose all of the elements of the claims, as required by 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1), and provides no apparent reason for modification to include such features.

For example, Stahmann fails to disclose or suggest " an insertable cardiac monitor (ICM) comprising: a housing configured for subcutaneous implantation within a patient, the housing having a length, a width, and a depth, wherein the length is greater than the width and the width is greater than the depth, and wherein the length is within a range from 40 millimeters (mm) to 60 mm," as recited by independent claim 1. Stahmann equally fails to disclose or suggest the similar recitations of independent claims 18, 27, and 29.
3 See, e.g., Applicant's originally filed specification, paragraphs [0046], [0052], and [0145].

4 See Hybritech Inc. v. Monoclonal Antibodies, Inc., 802 F.2d 1367, 231 USPQ 81 (CAFC 1986) ("it is axiomatic that for prior art to anticipate under 102 it has to meet every element of the claimed invention").

5 Id. See also Lewmar Marine, Inc. v. Barient, Inc. 827 F.2d 744, 3 USPQ2d 1766 (CAFC 1987); In re Bond, 910 F.2d 831, 15 USPQ2d 1566 (CAFC 1990); C.R. Bard, Inc. v. MP Systems, Inc., 157 F.3d 1340,48 USPQ2d 1225 (CAFC 1998); Oney v. Ratliff, 182 F.3d 893, 51 USPQ2d 1697 (CAFC 1999); Apple Computer, Inc. v. Articulate Systems, Inc., 234 F.3d 14, 57 USPQ2d 1057 (CAFC 2000).

The Office Action cited paragraph [0266] of Stahmann as allegedly disclosing a "housing having a length, a width, and a depth, wherein the length is greater than the width and the width is greater than the depth, and wherein the length is within a range from 40 millimeters (mm) to 60 mm." However, paragraph [0266] of Stahmann does not disclose a length of the housing, much less that the length of the housing "is within range from 40 millimeters (mm) to 60 mm," as claimed. Instead, paragraph [0266] of Stahmann states "[t]he housing 531 may resemble that of a conventional implantable ICD, is approximately 20-100 cc in volume, with a thickness of

0.4 to 2 cm and with a surface area on each face of approximately 30 to 100 cm2."6 None of these dimensions described by Stahmann is length of a housing, nor do they necessitate a particular range of housing lengths.
Nor is a length of the housing within a range from 40 mm to 60 mm inherent in the

dimensions described by Stahmann. Even if a length within a range from 40 mm to 60 mm (not disclosed by Stahmann) could result in a surface area greater than 30 cm2 when multiplied a given width (also not disclosed by Stahmann), such a length is not necessarily present in the device and surface area disclosed by Stahmann. The fact that a certain result or characteristic may occur or be present in the prior art is not sufficient to establish the inherency of that result or characteristic.7 "In relying upon the theory of inherency, the examiner must provide a basis in fact and/or technical reasoning to reasonably support the determination that the allegedly inherent characteristic necessarily flows from the teachings of the applied prior art."8

For at least the reasons discussed above, independent claims 1, 18, 27, and 29 are patentable over Stahmann. The dependent claims, i.e., claims 2-17, 19-26, 28, and 30, incorporate the requirements of the respective independent claims.9 Accordingly, the dependent claims are likewise patentable. Moreover, the dependent claims include a number of features likewise not disclosed or suggested by Stahmann.

For example, Stahmann does not disclose or suggest "processing circuitry configured to: periodically determine a respective value for each of a plurality of physiological parameters based on one or more of [] heart sounds or [] ECG; output trends of the periodically determined values of the physiological parameters at the remote computing device; and determine whether to
6 Emphasis added.
7 In re Rjckaert, 9 F.3d 1531, 1534, 28 USPQ2d 1955, 1957 (Fed. Cir. 1993).
8 Ex parte Levy, 17 USPQ2d 1461, 1464 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1990) (emphasis in original).

present an indication of a [heart failure] event based on an analysis of the trends of the periodically determined values of the physiological parameters," as recited by claim 2, or the similar recitations of claim 19. The Office Action cited paragraph [0972] of Stahmann as allegedly disclosing this feature. However, paragraph [0972] of Stahmann does not mention heart failure, much less disclose determining whether to present an indication of a heart failure event based on an analysis of trends of periodically determined values of the physiological parameters.

As another example, Stahmann does not disclose or suggest that "the indication of the cardiac event comprises an indication of a risk of the cardiac event," as recited by claims 3 and 20. The Office Action cited paragraphs [1409]-[1410] of Stahmann as allegedly disclosing this feature. However, paragraphs [1409]-[ 1410] of Stahmann do not mention risk, and instead describe determining presence or absence of a disease or disorder. For example, paragraph [1410] describes "[i]f changes in the conditions indicative of physiological changes or symptoms caused by the disease are consistent with threshold levels, a presence of the disease or disorder may be determined."

As another example, Stahmann does not disclose or suggest that "a volume of the ICM is less than 1.5 cubic centimeters," as recited by claim 17. The Office Action alleged that this feature was disclosed in paragraph [0266] of Stahmann. However, directly contrary to claim 17, paragraph [0266] of Stahmann states "[t]he housing 531 . . . is approximately 20-100 cc in volume."

Stahmann fails to disclose each and every recitation set forth in claims 1-30. For at least these reasons, the Office has failed to establish a primafacie case for anticipation of Applicant's claims 1-30 under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1). Applicant therefore respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of this rejection.
All claims in this application are in condition for allowance. Applicant does not

acquiesce as to any assertion in the Office Action with respect to the cited art or to Applicant's claims. Applicant's silence with respect to any assertion in the Office Action should not be interpreted as Applicant's acquiescence thereto. Applicant reserves the right to comment further with respect to the applied references and any pending claim in a future Amendment, Response, or on appeal. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and prompt allowance of all pending claims.

While several distinctions have been noted over the art of record, Applicant notes that there may be several other limitations that are neither taught nor suggested by the art of record. Applicant expressly reserves all rights and arguments with respect to distinctions not explicitly noted herein. To the extent that any particular statement or argument by the Office in the pending Office Action has not been explicitly addressed herein, the same should not be construed as an acquiescence or admission by the Applicant that such statements or arguments by the Office are accurate and proper.
